html:
In 1993 newly independent Uzbekistan passed a law to replace the Cyrillic alphabet with a Latin one for the Uzbek language. More than thirty years later the change is still unfinished, and both scripts are used side by side.

Uzbek changed scripts three times in the 20th century. It was written in Arabic script until the late 1920s, then in a Soviet Latin alphabet, then from 1940 in Cyrillic, as Moscow moved its Turkic peoples onto Cyrillic. After independence Latin letters were a sign of turning away from Russia and toward Turkey and the wider world. The 1993 alphabet was revised in 1995, and the deadline for the switch was pushed back again and again.

Schools teach in Latin, and street signs and much official writing use it, but many older people, newspapers and websites still use Cyrillic, and debates over letters such as oʻ and gʻ go on. Kazakhstan began its own move to Latin script in 2017, and Turkmenistan and Azerbaijan switched in the 1990s. Compare Mongolia, which kept Cyrillic.
